doc.title: Ray Vega interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 20, 2023

title: Telling a story with a set: the Post Bop Ensemble, Ray Barretto and reading the room
summary: Vega describes his UVM Post Bop Ensemble, sequencing sets like Ray Barretto's albums, and switching tunes on a gig to suit the audience.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah, yeah, yeah. I recently played with Roy McCurdy, his last drummer. I did a West Coast thing with him up the Pacific Northwest. We talked about all of that stuff. You connect with the audience. It’s important that we do that. And that doesn’t mean that we’re not presenting art music because it is art music. But let them see the humanity of the musician on stage. Unless you are just so so so shy that you can’t speak. I get it. But we don’t talk to our students about that. I talk to my students about, because I have one group at school, it’s called the Post Bop Ensemble. That’s the name of the group. I would have never called it that. But what these guys do is they come in and I’ll bring in some music for them to start but their job is to bring in music and eventually start rehearsing © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

that band like a band and I oversee the rehearsal. And these kids, first things first. Maybe one or two of them are music majors, the rest of them are engineers, astrophysicists, neuroscientists, all sorts of stuff. And these cats are on the case. We just graduated a young woman trombonist, an anthropology major. But she was a double major in music. So we got these kids that are coming in that are really brilliant but I have them develop the sets. And then when we’re going to do a recital I tell them okay now we’ve got to tell our story. You just can’t start and everything be at one level, you’ve got to go through peaks and valleys so the audience can really enjoy the complete presentation. Now where did I get that from? I got that from listening to records, from listening to albums. I remember working with Ray Barretto’s band, this was Ray Barretto’s jazz group New World Spirit and we’d go into the studio and then he’d want to come to the house, to my house with a bunch of different cassettes of different sequences of — and we would sit there and go man, no, let’s try something different. And he would sit there with the cassette and go let’s try something — ‘cause it was so important for him as an artist to be able to tell the story of what he wanted to tell. And so since the audience in a situation like a recital doesn’t have the power to hit shuffle, you have to tell them a story. You have to. So I talk to them about that and I always tell them, because there’s a place in town that does jam sessions on Wednesday nights and they have jazz on Thursday, Friday and Saturday. And a lot of these kids get to go in there, and I tell them look at your audience man. Yeah you know what you want to play, and be prepared to play it, but look at the sequence of compositions, look at the sequence of compositions because you want to be able to tell that particular crowd what’s going on. Like for instance yesterday we played, I forget what we started out the gig, but we started out the gig with whatever, I forget what it was. And we were going to go into Duke Ellington’s “Azure” I think that’s how you pronounce it. A-Z-U-R-E. But I knew that it wasn’t the right thing. I said, “Na, na, na, let’s switch it up immediately.” I said, “Let’s pull something else out and put it in its place.” Because you’ve got to read the audience. You know that one, okay let’s change the tempos around. It’s important to do that because the music isn’t just the notes it’s the complete and total package. You know? And mind you be — what’s the word — be sensitive to the audience too. You know, be sensitive.
That’s just me. I’m not saying everybody’s got to do it.
